title: What Makes a Life Meaningful?
objective: After this level you can weigh views of meaning in life that locate it in God's purpose, in what you care about, or in Susan Wolf's mix of caring and real worth.
summary: Supernaturalists find meaning in God’s purpose, subjectivists in what you care about, and Susan Wolf in caring about what is truly worthwhile; each view faces a serious objection.

cards.headline: One person spends years curing a disease. Another builds a giant ball of string.
cards.body: Both love what they do. Are both lives equally meaningful? Philosophers give three main answers, and the ball of string is a famous test case.

cards.headline: Meaning from God’s purpose
cards.body: Supernaturalists hold that meaning needs a spiritual realm. Some, such as William Lane Craig, argue that only God’s purpose could ground the objective values a meaningful life needs. Critics, following Kurt Baier, reply that being created for a purpose would degrade us: we’d be expected to serve the aims of a superior being, a bit like a well-made tool.

cards.headline: Meaning from caring
cards.body: Subjectivists say meaning varies from person to person. For Harry Frankfurt, a life is meaningful to the extent that you care about or love something. That respects your own passions. The objection is the ball of string: critics such as Susan Wolf ask whether devotion to a pointless project could really make a life meaningful, however much it’s loved.

cards.headline: Wolf’s mix
cards.body: Wolf’s own view is a hybrid: “Meaning arises when subjective attraction meets objective attractiveness.” You have to care, and what you care about has to be truly worth caring about. Love something worthless, or do something worthwhile without caring, and no meaning accrues. Critics ask who decides what’s objectively worthwhile, and that question is still debated.

cards.headline: What Makes a Life Meaningful?: the big picture
learned: Subjectivism: meaning from what you care about
Each view faces a serious objection

questions.prompt: Match each philosopher with his or her view of meaning in life.
questions.explanation: Craig argues only God’s purpose could ground meaning, Frankfurt says meaning comes from caring about or loving something, Wolf’s view is a hybrid, and Baier warned we’d be like a well-made tool.

questions.prompt: Lee spends years at a charity that helps many people, but she finds the work pointless and doesn’t care about it. What would Wolf say?

options.label: Her work gives her life full meaning, since it’s worthwhile
It adds no meaning on her view, because Lee doesn’t care about it
It’s meaningful as long as Lee is paid
options.rationale: Pay isn’t part of Wolf’s view.

options.label: Only God can say whether it’s meaningful

questions.explanation: On Wolf’s hybrid, a worthwhile project you don’t care about yields no meaning; both halves are needed.

questions.prompt: Using Level 1, why can’t a laboratory experiment settle whether building a giant ball of string makes a life meaningful?

options.label: The string is too long and tangled to measure
Nobody has ever built a big enough ball of string
options.rationale: The problem would remain if they had.

options.label: It asks what is valuable, which no experiment alone can show

questions.explanation: An experiment can show what people feel, but not whether a project is truly worth caring about.
